title: Comments of Defenders of Wildlife re the Preliminary Permit Application for the Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute and Infrastructure Hub Project under P-15423.

Christopher Brosman
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street NE, Room 1A
Washington, DC 20426

Re:    DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC, Preliminary Permit Application, Upper Cook Inlet (East Foreland
       Corridor), Alaska
       Project Number: P-15423-000

VIA FERC eFILING

Dear Mr. Brosman,

Established in 1947, Defenders of Wildlife is a national nonprofit conservation organization dedicated to
the protection of flora and fauna in its native habitat. Defenders has 1.8 million members and
supporters, including more than 4,300 in Alaska. We have long advocated for the conservation of
Alaska’s wildlife and habitat, including endangered Cook Inlet beluga whales and threatened northern
sea otters. Defenders appreciates this opportunity to comment on the above-referenced preliminary
permit application.

We understand that DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC (DeepGreen) seeks a preliminary permit under
section 4(f) of the Federal Power Act to study a project in the East Foreland corridor of Upper Cook Inlet.
The project would consist of approximately 330 to 350 marine hydrokinetic turbines, 66 subsea compute
pods, and an approximately 3.5-mile, 115 kV subsea cable landing in the Nikiski Industrial Corridor. 1
Press reports describe a project corridor of roughly 1,650 acres at depths of 45 to 166 feet and a four-
year study program.2 The notice does not identify any protected species or critical habitat, and the public
record we have reviewed does not describe the vessels, equipment, or acoustic sources studies
authorized under an FPA preliminary permit would use.

Two marine mammals call for particular attention. Cook Inlet belugas are listed as endangered under the
Endangered Species Act (ESA), and the project area lies within their designated critical habitat. Northern
sea otters are protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA), and the Southwest Alaska
distinct population segment, which occupies western Cook Inlet, is listed as threatened under the ESA
with designated critical habitat in lower Cook Inlet. Both statutes bear on this application.

Under the ESA, federal agencies must ensure “that any action authorized, funded, or carried out is not
likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any endangered species or threatened species or result in

000).

                     National Headquarters

the destruction or adverse modification of [critical habitat].”3 The Commission must review its actions at
the earliest possible time to determine whether they may affect listed species or critical habitat, and
consult with the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) for belugas and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife
Service (FWS) for sea otters if they may affect these species.4 A preliminary permit would be the
Commission’s first action in this proceeding, and the studies it would require would be the first in-water
activity. Although the Commission has held that the issuance of a preliminary permit does not require
ESA Section 7 consultation because it is “not an action likely to affect any endangered species or their
habitat,” we disagree.

The Commission’s conclusion that consultation is unnecessary is contrary to the established case law.
An agency may avoid Section 7’s consultation requirement only if it determines that its action will have
“no effect” on listed species or critical habitat.5 As the Ninth Circuit has explained, any possible effect,
whether beneficial, benign, adverse or of an undetermined character triggers consultation.6
Furthermore, the specific facts presented here—a project in navigable waters within designated Cook
Inlet beluga whale critical habitat where field studies will, at a minimum, foreseeably affect the whales
through noise—require consultation because the Commission cannot find that there will be “no effects”
on listed wildlife or critical habitat. Although the permit will not authorize any construction, DeepGreen
cannot conduct field studies without the preliminary permit establishing its priority and purpose, and, as
explained below, the studies themselves will affect beluga whales.

Additionally, under the MMPA it is unlawful to “take,” or “harass, hunt, capture, or kill, or attempt to
harass, hunt, capture, or kill any marine mammal.”7 Harassment is divided into “Level A” (any act with
the potential to injure a marine mammal) and “Level B” (acts with the potential to disturb, but not injure,
a marine mammal by disrupting behavioral patterns).8 NMFS authorizes incidental take of cetaceans
such as belugas, and FWS authorizes incidental take of sea otters. Either agency may authorize
incidental take for up to five years by regulation, or incidental harassment for up to one year, but only on
findings of small numbers, negligible impact, and no unmitigable adverse impact on subsistence uses,
and only with measures that effect the least practicable adverse impact.9 A one-year Incidental
Harassment Authorization (IHA) covers harassment only.10 The applicant has not said which
authorizations it will seek from either agency.

Cook Inlet Beluga Whales

Cook Inlet belugas were listed as depleted under the MMPA in 200011 and as endangered under the ESA
in 2008.12 NMFS designated critical habitat in 2011.13 The most recent abundance estimate we have
located is 331 animals (2022; range 290 to 386). The Marine Mammal Commission cautions that the
population’s low growth rate, combined with increasing human activity in beluga habitat, raises
significant concern about whether it can recover.14

The critical habitat designation identified the following physical or biological features essential to
conservation (also known as primary constituent elements (PCEs)):

       (1) Intertidal and subtidal waters of Cook Inlet with depths less than 30 feet (MLLW)(9.1 m)
       and within 5 miles (8 km) of high and medium flow anadromous fish streams.
       (2) Primary prey species consisting of four species of Pacific salmon (Chinook, sockeye,
       chum, and coho), Pacific eulachon, Pacific cod, walleye pollock, saffron cod, and yellowfin
       sole.
       (3) Waters free of toxins or other agents of a type and amount harmful to Cook Inlet beluga
       whales.
       (4) Unrestricted passage within or between the critical habitat areas.
       (5) Waters with in-water noise below levels resulting in the abandonment of critical habitat
       areas by Cook Inlet beluga whales.15

The East Foreland and Nikiski reach lies within Area 2 of the designated critical habitat, which includes
all marine waters of Cook Inlet south of the line from the mouth of Threemile Creek to Point Possession
and north of 60°15′ N.16 Each of the five PCEs is implicated by this proposal.

Noise (PCE 5). In 2016, NMFS completed a Recovery Plan that identifies noise as a significant threat to
recovery, of high concern relative to other threats.17 Belugas’ high auditory sensitivity, wide frequency
bandwidth, and dependence on sound to navigate, communicate, and find prey make them vulnerable to

noise, which can mask their signals or, if intense, lead to hearing impairment.18 The Recovery Plan
concluded that “there is sufficient evidence to suggest that the reproductive success and survival of
cetaceans can be negatively impacted by noise.”19 If it receives a preliminary license, DeepGreen would
add noise to Cook Inlet via survey and vessel traffic; thereafter, if it receives a license and proceeds with
construction, it will add noise via installation of hundreds of turbine cradles and a cable landing, and,
unlike a conventional construction project, continuous operational noise from 330 to 350 turbines and
66 computer pods running around the clock. Chronic sources raise the background noise level over long
periods. Scientists who analyzed 8,756 hours of recordings in Cook Inlet found anthropogenic noise on
every day sampled and concluded that several sources could chronically mask beluga communication
and hearing across most locations and months sampled.20 The application offers no source levels,
propagation modeling, or acoustic baseline.

Passage and shallow nearshore waters (PCEs 1 and 4). The array and cable would occupy a corridor that
press reports describe as the narrowest point of the inlet.21 The application does not show how
“unrestricted passage” would be preserved. The cable landing would cross shallow nearshore waters,
and the applicant must show whether those waters are less than 30 feet deep and within 5 miles of
anadromous streams, and how trenching or drilling would be done and when.

Prey (PCE 2). The listed prey include Chinook, sockeye, chum, and coho salmon and eulachon, which
migrate through this reach. Noise, electromagnetic fields from a 115 kV cable, turbine passage, scour
and sediment changes, and thermal or chemical releases could each alter prey behavior or distribution.
None is assessed. In the parallel DeepGreen proceeding in Maine, NMFS has reportedly told the
Commission that ESA and essential fish habitat consultations may be necessary,22 and the same
coordination should occur here.

Toxins and heat (PCE 3). Essentially all the electricity consumed by the compute load of up to 100
megawatts would be released as heat, and the application describes passive cooling by direct exchange

with inlet water. DeepGreen has not disclosed its materials and fluids, its thermal discharge, or its spill
prevention measures.

Cumulative effects. These effects would add to existing stressors in the same reach, including industrial
and vessel traffic at Nikiski and the planned Cook Inlet PowerLink submarine transmission line, to which
the applicant says its project would connect.23

Northern Sea Otters

Northern sea otters in Alaska are managed as three stocks. The Southwest Alaska stock, which includes
western Cook Inlet, was listed as threatened under the ESA in 2005, and FWS designated critical habitat
in 2009, including a unit that reaches western lower Cook Inlet as far north as Tuxedni Bay.24 The
Southcentral Alaska stock, which includes the Kenai Peninsula coast, eastern Cook Inlet, and Kachemak
Bay, is not listed under the ESA but is protected under the MMPA. FWS estimated about 9,152 sea otters
in eastern Cook Inlet in 2017.25 The Nikiski shoreline is on the eastern side of the inlet. The application
does not say whether sea otters occur in the East Foreland corridor, and we are not aware of recent
survey data for that shoreline. It also does not say whether project vessels, staging areas, or installation
work would reach waters used by the Southwest Alaska stock or its critical habitat across the inlet.
These are threshold questions that the applicant must answer with surveys and that FWS must evaluate.

FWS’s recent proposed IHAs show what a sea otter analysis requires and where the agency’s standards
are uneven. In 2024, FWS proposed an IHA for construction of a seaplane base in Sitka (Southeast Alaska
stock), with up to 36 takes by Level B harassment.26 In August 2026, FWS proposed an IHA for harbor pile
driving in Unalaska (Southwest Alaska stock), with up to 32 instances of Level A and 273 instances of
Level B harassment affecting up to 112 sea otters.27 Both are small, localized harbor projects (18 days of
pile-driving activity in Sitka and up to 100 days in Unalaska).28 DeepGreen’s proposal is far larger and far
less defined. The following issues are drawn from those notices.

Noise thresholds and chronic exposure. Exposure to noise can interrupt feeding, nursing and resting,
forcing the otters to burn more energy and eat more to make up the difference. FWS applies a 160 dB re 1
µPa Level B threshold to both impulsive and nonimpulsive underwater sound and explained that NMFS’s

120 dB threshold for continuous noise is not appropriate for sea otters because it rests on gray whale
responses and 1980s playback studies in which southern sea otters showed no disturbance.29 In 2026,
FWS also stated that it is still evaluating NMFS’s 2024 auditory injury criteria.30 These thresholds were
applied to discrete construction events. They have not been tested against continuous operation of
hundreds of turbines and dozens of compute pods for years. If sea otters occur near the site, chronic
exposure must be evaluated explicitly rather than assumed to follow short-term pile-driving findings.
Behavior at low noise levels and movement corridors. FWS’s 2024 notice recounts that in Cook Inlet, sea
otters drifting toward an active offshore drilling rig swam to avoid a close approach within about 500
meters despite near-ambient noise levels, and that sea otters in Alaska avoid areas with heavy vessel
traffic.31 FWS treats abandoning a feeding area and ceasing to use movement corridors as Level B
harassment, and the Unalaska analysis assumed that up to 12 sea otters per day travel through a
channel overlapping the noise zone.32 Presence and structure, not only decibel levels, can displace
otters. Avoiding productive feeding corridors cuts the otters off from food and resting areas and can
separate mothers from pups. The applicant should identify any sea otter feeding areas and travel
corridors in and around the project area.

Vessel strikes and vessel protocols. A collision can cause massive trauma, hemorrhaging, broken bones,
or propeller lacerations that kill or seriously injure an otter. FWS documents vessel-strike mortality in all
three Alaska stocks, including 10 of 483 sea otter deaths with an identifiable cause during 2002–2012.33
The Sitka proposal would require vessels to remain at least 500 meters from rafts of ten or more sea
otters and 100 meters from all other sea otters, and to avoid alongshore travel in water shallower than 20
meters whenever practicable.34 The Unalaska proposal requires a 100-meter minimum distance.35 Four
years of survey work, installation, and maintenance, plus nearshore cable work, call for a vessel plan at
least this protective.

Habitat and prey. FWS describes sea otter habitat as benthic invertebrates, shallow rocky areas, and
kelp, and notes that sea otters are most commonly found within the 40-meter (131-foot) depth contour.36
Press reports place this project at depths of 45 to 166 feet, so a large part of its depth range lies within
the depths FWS treats as primary sea otter habitat where otters are present. FWS also recognizes that

pile driving, vibration, and sedimentation can affect prey and reduce foraging efficiency, and the Sitka
project would permanently remove 1.3 acres of habitat.37 DeepGreen would place a far larger footprint,
with scour and sediment effects, on the seabed. Sea otters depend on their fur for insulation and are
highly vulnerable to oil and other contaminants; thousands of Southcentral stock sea otters died after
the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill.38 The application discloses no measures to prevent releases of fuel,
fluids, or other contaminants. Sediment, vibrations and permanent structures reduce the benthic
invertebrates otters eat, clould the water they hunt in and remove foraging habitat, all causing otters to
spend more energy finding less-preferred prey.

Cumulative Effects. DeepGreen proposes multi-year studies followed, if licensed, by long-term
continuous operation. An IHA cannot cover chronic exposure over that span, or serious injury or mortality
from turbine strikes, cable entanglement, or vessel collisions. Repeated disturbances, vessel traffic and
contaminants layered on one another produce chronic stress that FWS links to weakened immune
function and lower body weight, which can reduce survival and reproduction. DeepGreen should identify
now which MMPA authorizations it expects to seek from FWS and NMFS, and the agencies should
coordinate on the combined effects on two protected species in the same area.

Requests

Defenders respectfully requests that the Commission:
     1. Deny the preliminary permit, or defer action until DeepGreen files a complete application that
        includes project coordinates, component dimensions and materials, a detailed study plan, and
        surveys of beluga and sea otter occurrence.
     2. Obtain official species lists and begin ESA section 7 consultation with NMFS (belugas) and FWS
        (sea otters) before issuing any preliminary permit.
     3. Require a study plan that identifies every in-water activity, vessel, and acoustic source, and the
        MMPA authorizations required, and condition any permit so that no in-water work begins until
        NMFS and FWS have completed consultation and issued those authorizations.
     4. If studies proceed, require measures at least as protective as the most protective recent agency
        authorizations, including halting work when belugas are seen in or approaching the Level B
        harassment zone, seasonal restrictions, and bubble curtains, as NMFS required of the Port of
        Anchorage;39 and a 30-meter sea otter shutdown zone and the Sitka vessel distances, with
        protected species observers and passive acoustic monitoring.

   5. Require baseline data before any license application is accepted: passive acoustic and visual
      beluga monitoring across seasons; sea otter surveys of the East Foreland shoreline, vessel
      routes, and staging areas; and prey and fish habitat surveys.
   6. Require assessments of noise in all phases, including chronic operational noise, as well as
      electromagnetic fields, thermal discharge, contaminants and spill risk, and a decommissioning
      plan.
   7. Consult with Tribes and Alaska Native organizations, including on subsistence use of sea otters,
      and incorporate Traditional Ecological Knowledge in study design.
   8. Evaluate cumulative effects with other planned and existing activities in the reach, including the
      Cook Inlet PowerLink and Nikiski industrial and vessel traffic.
Feel free to contact us with questions or comments that you may have.
